Purpose and scope

This policy sets out how Alderbridge Care Group orders, receives and holds medication stock safely. It applies to every site holding medication stock, including controlled drugs, for resident use.

Policy statement

Medication stock is ordered, received and stored through a controlled, auditable process at every stage, so that the amount held matches what has genuinely been prescribed and administered, and any discrepancy is identified quickly rather than accumulating unnoticed.

Definitions

**Electronic ordering system** the system that has replaced the paper order book for recording and submitting every medication order, timestamped and countersigned digitally. **Stock count** the physical count of medication held against the electronic ordering system and administration records. **Urgent flag** the function used in place of a verbal emergency order when a resident's supply unexpectedly runs low.

Roles and responsibilities

**The registered manager** countersigns every order digitally in the electronic ordering system before it is sent. **The nominated senior carer** completes the weekly stock count and reconciles it against the electronic ordering system. **The supplying pharmacy** confirms receipt of each order, including any urgent-flagged order, the same day.

Interaction with other Alderbridge policies

This policy works alongside the Safe Administration of Medication Policy and Controlled Drugs Procedure (governing how counted stock is then administered) and the Records Retention Schedule (governing how long electronic ordering and stock count records are kept).

Worked example

A worked example illustrates the urgent-flag route. A resident's regular supply is found to be two days short during a Friday evening stock check. The senior carer raises an urgent flag in the electronic ordering system, the pharmacy confirms same-day dispatch, and delivery arrives Saturday morning with the digital record already complete and countersigned, removing the retrospective paperwork step the previous version required.

Frequently asked questions

**Why was the verbal emergency order removed?** A review found the retrospective paperwork it required was sometimes delayed past the 24-hour window; the urgent flag produces a complete digital record at the moment the order is raised, closing that gap. **Can a family member bring in a resident's own medication instead of it being ordered through the pharmacy?** No, all resident medication is ordered through the approved pharmacy route via the electronic ordering system so that stock records remain accurate and complete.

Training and competency

Senior carers complete electronic ordering system and stock-count training before being authorised to hold the controlled drugs cabinet key, refreshed annually alongside the wider medication competency assessment.

Monitoring and compliance

Stock count accuracy and any discrepancy is reviewed monthly by the registered manager as part of the wider medication audit, now incorporating the monthly controlled-drugs reconciliation cross-check, with persistent discrepancies escalated to the Quality Lead.

Record keeping and retention

Electronic ordering system entries and stock count records are retained per the Records Retention Schedule and made available to CQC inspectors on request.

Purpose and scope

This plan sets out how Alderbridge Care Group prepares for, responds to, and recovers from a major
emergency affecting a site, now including a dedicated annex covering a pandemic or significant supply
chain disruption affecting the wider organisation rather than a single site alone. It applies to every site.

Policy statement

Alderbridge treats emergency preparedness as a continuous discipline; this version extends that discipline
to a sector-wide emergency, a pandemic or a significant supply chain disruption, that may affect every
Alderbridge site simultaneously rather than one site in isolation, requiring a different, organisation-wide
coordination approach to the single-site mutual aid model this plan already describes.

Definitions

**Major emergency** an incident causing significant disruption to safe care delivery. **Regional mutual
aid** the arrangement coordinating support between sites within a region. **Sector-wide emergency** the
new category, introduced in this version, covering a pandemic, a national supply chain disruption, or
another event affecting multiple or all Alderbridge sites simultaneously, requiring organisation-level rather
than purely regional or site-level coordination. **Critical supply** the new term, introduced in this version,
for an item, such as personal protective equipment or a specific medication category, whose unavailability
would directly compromise safe care.

**The registered manager** holds overall responsibility for their site's own emergency plan and now also
monitors local critical supply levels. **The regional manager** coordinates mutual aid within their region.
**The Health and Safety Lead**, in an expanded role introduced in this version, coordinates the
organisation-wide response to a sector-wide emergency, including critical supply allocation across regions,
and chairs the new organisation-level emergency coordination group for such an event.

Resident and family involvement in medication decisions

Wherever a resident has capacity, they are involved directly in decisions about their own medication; where capacity is lacking, family or an advocate is involved in a best-interests process rather than a purely clinical decision being made without any input beyond the care team itself.

Medication reconciliation on admission and transfer

Every resident's full medication list is reconciled against the prescribing GP's own record at admission, and again at any hospital transfer in either direction, since a mismatch between what a resident is believed to be taking and what they are actually prescribed is one of the most common sources of a serious medication error. This reconciliation is completed by a registered nurse or the registered manager, never left solely to an informal handover conversation.

Managing a medication change communicated verbally

Where a GP communicates a medication change verbally, this is confirmed in writing before the change is actually implemented, except in a genuine emergency where immediate action is clinically necessary; a verbal instruction alone is not treated as sufficient authority for an ongoing change to a resident's regular medication regimen.

End of life medication considerations

Handling a medication supply disruption

Where a national or regional medication supply issue affects a resident's regular prescription, the GP and pharmacy work together to identify a suitable alternative promptly, and the registered manager ensures the resident and family are kept informed of any change this makes necessary.

Cross-site consistency and local flexibility

While the medication policy suite applies identically across every Alderbridge site, a site's own physical layout may shape exactly how a specific step is carried out in practice; this local variation is documented in the site's own standard operating procedure without altering the underlying policy requirement itself.

Auditing the suite as a whole

Beyond auditing each specific policy on its own terms, the Quality Lead conducts an annual whole-suite audit, sampling a cross-section of resident records across every specific medication activity to confirm the suite functions coherently for a resident whose care genuinely spans several of its specific policies at once, rather than each policy passing its own individual audit while a gap remains at the boundary between them.

Learning from a near miss across the suite

A near miss, however minor, is treated as valuable information about where the suite's practical application might be strengthened, not simply logged and forgotten once no harm has resulted; a recurring near-miss pattern in a specific activity, identified through the severity trend analysis, often points to a genuine gap in training, resourcing, or the specific policy's own clarity that is worth addressing proactively.

Reviewing this overarching policy's own effectiveness

Beyond the specific policy reviews and the whole-suite audit, the Board periodically considers whether the medication framework as a whole, including this overarching document's own structure and severity classification appendix, remains fit for purpose, informed by external benchmarking against current clinical and regulatory guidance.

Purpose and scope

This policy sets out how Alderbridge Care Group supports a resident receiving end of life care, and their family, with dignity and appropriate clinical input. It applies to every site.

Policy statement

End of life care focuses on comfort, dignity and the resident's own wishes wherever these are known, working closely with the resident's GP, any involved palliative care team, and the family, so that the resident's final period of life is supported as they and their family would wish.

DNACPR decisions

A Do Not Attempt Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation decision, where made, is documented on the appropriate form, signed by the resident's GP, and kept readily accessible in the resident's room so that it can be acted on immediately by any responding staff member or emergency service. This section now appears early in the document, reflecting that it is often the first thing staff need to check during a clinical emergency.

Symptom management

Pain and other symptoms are managed in line with the resident's care plan and GP or palliative team guidance, with staff trained to recognise a change in symptoms that may need a clinical review rather than waiting for the next scheduled visit. This section, too, now appears earlier in the document than in the previous version, alongside DNACPR, given how often the two are consulted together.

Advance care planning

Where a resident has capacity, staff encourage an early conversation about their wishes for end of life care, recorded in an advance care plan and reviewed as circumstances change; where a resident lacks capacity, the plan is developed with family and clinical input in the resident's best interests.

Policy statement

own medication, since retaining this level of independence matters to a resident's own sense of control
over their daily life, balanced against a proportionate risk assessment.

Definitions

**Self-administration** a resident managing and taking their own medication themselves, rather than a
staff member administering it. **Capacity and risk assessment** the assessment completed before
self-administration begins for any self-administered medication, with no exempted category under this
version, reviewed annually with an additional quarterly re-review. **Topical medication** a cream, ointment

medication.

begins, for every medication category, and schedules the new quarterly re-review. **The resident's GP or
a pharmacist** contributes clinical input to the assessment where relevant. **Care staff** monitor for any
sign that self-administration is no longer safe, reporting a concern to the registered manager rather than
deciding themselves to withdraw the arrangement.

Supersedes the version effective 1 June 2023. Replaces the paper order book with the electronic ordering system and removes the verbal emergency-order allowance in favour of an urgent-flag function with same-day pharmacy confirmation; adds a monthly controlled-drugs reconciliation cross-check.

Purpose and scope

This policy sets out how Alderbridge Care Group orders, receives and holds medication stock safely. It applies to every site holding medication stock, including controlled drugs, for resident use.

Policy statement

Medication stock is ordered, received and stored through a controlled, auditable process at every stage, so that the amount held matches what has genuinely been prescribed and administered, and any discrepancy is identified quickly rather than accumulating unnoticed.

Definitions

**Electronic ordering system** the system that has replaced the paper order book for recording and submitting every medication order, timestamped and countersigned digitally. **Stock count** the physical count of medication held against the electronic ordering system and administration records. **Urgent flag** the function used in place of a verbal emergency order when a resident's supply unexpectedly runs low.

Roles and responsibilities

**The registered manager** countersigns every order digitally in the electronic ordering system before it is sent. **The nominated senior carer** completes the weekly stock count and reconciles it against the electronic ordering system. **The supplying pharmacy** confirms receipt of each order, including any urgent-flagged order, the same day.

Worked example

A worked example illustrates the urgent-flag route. A resident's regular supply is found to be two days short during a Friday evening stock check. The senior carer raises an urgent flag in the electronic ordering system, the pharmacy confirms same-day dispatch, and delivery arrives Saturday morning with the digital record already complete and countersigned, removing the retrospective paperwork step the previous version required.

Frequently asked questions

**Why was the verbal emergency order removed?** A review found the retrospective paperwork it required was sometimes delayed past the 24-hour window; the urgent flag produces a complete digital record at the moment the order is raised, closing that gap. **Can a family member bring in a resident's own medication instead of it being ordered through the pharmacy?** No, all resident medication is ordered through the approved pharmacy route via the electronic ordering system so that stock records remain accurate and complete.

Training and competency

Senior carers complete electronic ordering system and stock-count training before being authorised to hold the controlled drugs cabinet key, refreshed annually alongside the wider medication competency assessment.

Monitoring and compliance

Stock count accuracy and any discrepancy is reviewed monthly by the registered manager as part of the wider medication audit, now incorporating the monthly controlled-drugs reconciliation cross-check, with persistent discrepancies escalated to the Quality Lead.

Record keeping and retention

Electronic ordering system entries and stock count records are retained per the Records Retention Schedule and made available to CQC inspectors on request.

Approval and review history

This policy was originally approved by the Chief Executive on 1 June 2023 and this version took effect 1 October 2025, superseding the earlier paper-based version.

Stock discrepancy investigation

Any stock discrepancy identified at a weekly count is investigated the same day by the registered manager, checking administration records first before considering whether an ordering or delivery error explains the gap, since most discrepancies trace back to a simple recording error rather than a genuine loss.

Exceptions and professional judgement

Where a genuinely urgent clinical need arises outside pharmacy opening hours, the on-call registered manager may authorise sourcing a single dose from a partner site's stock, recorded in both sites' order books and reconciled at the next stock count.

Local and regional variations

Harbour View's larger resident population means its weekly stock count is split across two senior carers working together, cross-checking each other's count, rather than a single senior carer counting alone as at the smaller sites.
